title: SeedLoader's external-key probe queries `where: { name }` on objects that have no `name` column — a hard INVALID_FILTER refusal per row, per pass
body:
Observation from the HotCRM multi-tenant acceptance in objectstack-ai/cloud#1350 (real `serve` boot, real 342-row seed). Not blocking anything — the seed completes and the counters are correct — but it produces a large volume of ERROR-level noise that reads exactly like a real failure, on every seeded boot and every per-organization replay.

## What is logged

For every object whose seed dataset declares an `externalId` other than `name`, and which has no `name` column, the loader's lookup chain tries `name` anyway:

```
Find operation starting {"object":"crm_contact","query":{"where":{"name":"priya.shah@lattice.example.com", ...}}}
[sql-driver] INVALID_FILTER — a WHERE column could not be resolved on 'crm_contact' ('name')
ERROR Find operation failed {"object":"crm_contact","error":{"message":"Filter on 'name' names a column that object 'crm_contact' has no column for, so the predicate never ran. ..."}}
```

Observed on `crm_contact` (externalId `email`), `crm_case` and `crm_task` (`subject`), `crm_knowledge_article` (`title`). The chain then falls through to `id`, and the correct `email` lookup that ran immediately before it is the one that answers — so the `name` attempt contributes nothing but the refusal.

## Why it is worth a line of code

Two costs, neither large on its own:

- **Volume and misdirection.** A single HotCRM replay emits hundreds of these at ERROR level. Anyone reading a seeded boot log — or an agent triaging one — sees a wall of "Find operation failed" and has to establish, by hand, that they are inert. It is the same class of hazard as a warning nobody reads, inverted: an error everybody must learn to ignore.
- **The fallback cannot work as written.** `name` is tried unconditionally rather than derived from the object's declared name field, so on these objects it is guaranteed to be refused rather than merely unmatched. The driver refuses (correctly — a filter on a nonexistent column can only match zero rows, so answering "no match" would be a lie), which means the attempt is not a cheap miss.

## Suggested shape

Ask the metadata registry for the object's name field before probing it, or skip the `name` leg entirely when the object declares no such column. Either removes the refusal without changing which lookup answers.

Filed as an observation, not a defect blocking work: no seed outcome changes.
